items.title: ASIC halts Remara's private credit products for TMD deficiencies
items.teaser: ASIC has slapped interim stop orders on Remara Investment Management's private credit products over deficiencies in its target market determination (TMD), claiming they were too risky for retail investors.
items.brief_text: ASIC has slapped interim stop orders on Remara Investment Management's private credit products over deficiencies in its target market determination (TMD), claiming they were too risky for retail investors. The three products - the 6 Month (Fixed and Variable) Account, 12 Month (Fixed and Variable) Account and At Call Account - sit under the Remara Cash Management Fund, a registered managed investment scheme. ASIC hit Remara and its trustee Melbourne Securities Corporation (MSC) with the interim design distribution orders (DDO) stop orders for 21 days unless revoked earlier. During this time, MSC will cease dealing in interests, issuing a product disclosure statement for, or providing general financial product advice to retail clients recommending an investment in, the fund's products. The fund has $39.9 million in assets under management at the end of December 2025. It invests in short-term notes linked to a pool of Australian credit investments that are AAA-rated, and investment-grade securitised and equivalent shadow-rated instruments, which are internal credit evaluations that assess the credit risk of issuers that do not have public ratings. They include public and private residential mortgage-backed securities, asset-backed securities and mortgage-backed securities. The fund may invest up to 100% of its assets in shadow-rated instruments.
items.ai_summary: ASIC halts Remara's private credit products due to inadequate target market determination for retail investors

items.title: FAAA calls for review of proposed data breach report deadline
items.teaser: The Financial Advice Association Australia’s submission to privacy reform consultation recommends clarifications including how certain points will work alongside existing regulations, and a review of the 72-hour data breach report deadline.
items.brief_text: The Financial Advice Association Australia has raised concerns over its members’ ability to meet a proposed 72-hour window to determine if a data breach should be reported and recommends in a submission to consultation on the Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill that the deadline be reviewed for small businesses. “Member feedback indicates that the practical difficulty lies not only in preparing a notification, but in determining within 72 hours whether an incident is reportable,” according to the submission. The difficulty lies on the possibility that the information required lies outside of the business and with a third-party provider, technology company or its licensee. The FAAA recommends clarification of when the 72-hour notification period commences and the guidance is provided around the circumstances in which entities may rely on the incomplete notification provisions. Financial advisers have access to clients’ most personal and sensitive information and are well placed to identify early signs of potential abuse being experienced by these clients. The FAAA wants further guidance on how this permitted general situation (PGS) will interact with an adviser’s existing legal duties of confidentiality.
items.ai_summary: FAAA seeks review of the 72-hour data breach reporting deadline for small businesses due to practical challenges

items.title: Treasury opens consultation for CSLR special levy
items.teaser: On 21 September, Treasury launched consultation on its proposed waterfall framework to fund the 2026-27 special levy after the financial advice sub-sector cap was exceeded by $170.3 million in the most recent revised estimates.
items.brief_text: On 21 September, Treasury launched consultation on its proposed waterfall framework to fund the 2026-27 special levy after the financial advice sub-sector cap was exceeded by $170.3 million in the most recent revised estimates. Flagged in Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino’s Press Club address last month , the waterfall model will see others within the related sector (in this case, financial services) cover the ballooning costs following comprehensive consultation with the industry earlier in the year aimed at making the CSLR more sustainable. “The framework seeks to allocate levy costs to the financial services sub ‑ sectors most closely connected to the losses giving rise to compensation claims, while limiting the risk that any single sub ‑ sector bears a levy burden that could adversely affect its financial sustainability and viability,” the minister said.
items.ai_summary: Treasury consults on a waterfall framework to fund the CSLR special levy following sector cap exceedance

items.title: 'Beyond warnings': ASIC to come down heavy on private credit
items.teaser: The corporate regulator has urged the private credit sector to uplift standards, noting participants should prepare for enforcement action if they fail to do so.
items.brief_text: The corporate regulator has urged the private credit sector to uplift standards, noting participants should prepare for enforcement action if they fail to do so. ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the regulator is now "beyond warnings" and pushed players to assess themselves against its 10 best practice principles. Constant said ASIC expects everyone in the investment chain - fund managers, deal underwriters and trustees right through to valuers, auditors and ratings agencies - to consistently meet their responsibilities. The recent collapse of property developer Bathla put a spotlight on the private credit sector, as investors pulled their money back from private credit exposures. Constant noted offering regular redemptions to investors while sitting on illiquid assets creates a structural mismatch that must be resolved. "Offering regular redemptions to investors while holding illiquid, multi-year property loans creates a fragile product design that breaks down under pressure - especially when coupled with loan "management practices" that rearrange deck chairs while the tide goes out and the boat risks running aground," she said. She added when property projects stall and credit vehicles freeze redemptions, the damage falls squarely on the real economy. "Contractors and trade subcontractors are left unpaid, homebuyers face the distressing prospect of losing their deposits, and superannuation members find their retirement savings locked away.
items.ai_summary: ASIC warns private credit sector to improve standards and prepare for enforcement action amid structural risks

items.title: Class action against Macquarie echoes soon-to-be-eliminated ‘but for’ determinations
items.teaser: A class action against Macquarie Investment Management over its role in the collapse of the Shield master fund claims it should compensate investors for investment returns they missed out on by not being invested somewhere else.
items.brief_text: The class action filed in the Supreme Court of Victoria this week by plaintiff lawyers Gordon Legal against Macquarie Investment Management over Macquarie’s role in the collapse of the Shield master fund has all the hallmarks of the controversial “but for” claims that the government is moving to remove from the Australian Financial Complaints Authority’s remit. Macquarie has already repaid $321 million to investors on its superannuation platform who lost money in the Shield collapse, to restore them to their initial capital position. Another platform operator, Netwealth, compensated investors in another failed managed investment scheme, First Guardian, to the tune of $100 million on a similar basis. Gordon Legal said in a media release that in Macquarie’s case this is not enough, and “investors have not been compensated for the growth their superannuation may have achieved if those funds had remained invested elsewhere during that time, or for the distress they have suffered”. “A core feature of superannuation is your super grows in value over time. An initial relatively small amount put into your super when you are 20 years old may grow significantly by the time you retire,” the law firm says on its website.
items.ai_summary: Class action against Macquarie highlights concerns over compensation for lost super growth despite initial capital repayment

items.title: Claude for advisers has regulators and competitors on alert
items.teaser: ASIC says it is closely monitoring developments such as the new Claude for financial advisers’ plugin – launched this week – and its potential implications for the Australian market. Incumbent tech vendors are also watching.
items.brief_text: The Australian Securities and Investments Commission says it is closely monitoring developments such as Anthropic’s Claude for financial advisers which was announced on 15 September. An ASIC spokesperson tells Professional Planner the regulator is monitoring developments alongside with peer regulators to assess possible implications for the Australian market. The new Claude product is currently available in the US via integrations with technology vendors such as Salesforce and Vanguard. Between clearing regulatory requirements and setting up data centres, among other things, Claude’s new feature may take two years to reach Australia, if it comes at all. That can get even more complicated if it involves super funds, as trustees would have to sign off on member data being shared with other technology services providers. Incumbent Australian tech vendors are also watching the offshore developments closely as a potential threat to the established order emerges. “I still feel it’ll be quite a few years probably before this happens in a meaningful scale. But I do feel it is inevitable at some point that advisers are going to want this capability,” Finura Group joint managing director Peter Worn tells Professional Planner . The benefit of using an LLM such as Claude is considerable, especially for firms currently using many different advice tech systems.
items.ai_summary: ASIC is monitoring AI developments like Claude for potential impacts on the Australian financial advice industry

items.title: Div 296 no hurdle to SMSF establishments, Class research finds
items.teaser: There’s never been more money in self-managed super funds than there is today, and the rate they’re being created has never been faster.
items.brief_text: More than 52,000 new SMSFs were established in FY26, the highest number ever recorded, according to new analysis by Class. The total number of funds surpassed 680,000, growth of 7.4 per cent on the year, also the highest total on record. Class chief executive Tim Steele says the growth has come despite Division 296 and new limits on residential property borrowing. “Firstly, I would say at a macro level, SMSFs have just had the strongest year on record,” Steele says. “Despite the kind of regulatory backdrop and potentially changes in relation to things like Div 296, SMSFs are more popular than they’ve ever been.” “The themes around control and flexibility, and people taking an interest and being engaged in their super, are already positive things,” Steele says. Steele says the Div 296 tax change has not deterred even younger members who may cross the $3 million threshold over their working lives. “I think it’s a problem they’d love to have,” Steele says. “When someone age 21 enters the workforce and is contributing 12.5 per cent of their super, that beautiful eighth wonder of the world, compound interest, will mean they can grow a material balance over their lifetime. “I just don’t think the potential risk of, at some stage in your life, having more than $3 million in super, is a deterrent.
items.ai_summary: SMSF establishment numbers hit record highs in FY26 despite regulatory challenges like Div 296

items.title: Named, but not accused: ASIC’s warning that isn’t a warning
items.teaser: When ASIC warns consumers to take care when dealing with a service provider but doesn’t explain to them why, it does not support informed decision-making. The information published should be sufficiently precise to let the reader understand what is known and what is not and why the warning has been issued.
items.brief_text: Imagine that your business appears on a consumer warning page published by ASIC. The page tells consumers to exercise “additional caution”. It sits within a regulatory campaign prompted by concerns that Australians are being pressured into switching their superannuation and exposed to significant losses. ASIC announces your inclusion in a media release and says it is putting industry participants “on notice”. But ASIC also says that naming your business should not be understood as indicating that any law has been broken, or even as reflecting upon you. What, then, is the public supposed to make of your name being on this list? That is the unresolved contradiction at the centre of ASIC’s list of businesses involved in superannuation lead generation. The List ASIC began publishing ‘the list’ in February 2026 as part of a review of advice licensees using lead-generation services. It initially named 44 entities and added another 19 in June. The list includes lead generators and referral partners, as well as advice licensees, corporate authorised representatives and financial advisers that have acquired leads since 1 July 2024. ASIC says some lead-generation practices may expose consumers to significant losses. Its accompanying warnings refer to high-pressure tactics, “free” superannuation health checks, claims that existing funds are underperforming, limited contact with an adviser, poor product disclosure and promises of unrealistic returns.
items.ai_summary: ASIC's list of superannuation lead generators includes businesses not accused of wrongdoing, raising questions about consumer warnings

items.title: Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech-Driven, Compliance-Led
items.teaser: Silvia Wade Founder of Mutual Paraplanning Services Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech Driven, Compliance Led For a long time, people in our profession have viewed paraplanners as note-takers and creators…
items.brief_text: Silvia Wade Founder of Mutual Paraplanning Services Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech Driven, Compliance Led For a long time, people in our profession have viewed paraplanners as note-takers and creators of Statements of Advice only after the strategy is set. But times have changed. That old view no longer reflects the present, or future of paraplanning. The modern paraplanner is both a strategic partner and a compliance gatekeeper within the advice preparation process As AI automation and other technology become the norm, the role of paraplanners is evolving in exciting ways. Technology is removing the repetitive, process-driven parts of our work, creating space for experienced paraplanners to become more strategic, proactive, and valuable to advice practices. And as AI accelerates meeting notes, data organisation, and SOA preparation, it frees paraplanners to focus on higher-value work. After all, an SOA is merely a format for delivering advice; it is not the advice itself. Someone must understand the client, explore suitable strategies, model outcomes, conduct research, and ensure the recommendations can be supported. That deeper work is where today’s paraplanners can contribute most Empty heading Strategic support and modelling The modern paraplanner can analyse, model, question, research, validate and collaborate.
items.ai_summary: Paraplanning is evolving into a strategic, tech-driven, and compliance-led role within financial advice practices

items.title: Court ruling highlights member benefits and disputes in intergenerational wealth transfer
items.teaser: In Topp, in the matter of McLennan Holdings Pty Limited (In Liq) [2026] FCA 1259, Justice Yaseen Shariff backed a court-appointed receiver’s decision not to pursue legal action against family members or a financial adviser over transactions that shifted millions of dollars from the retirement benefits of elderly fund…
items.brief_text: In Topp, in the matter of McLennan Holdings Pty Limited (In Liq) [2026] FCA 1259 , Justice Yaseen Shariff backed a court-appointed receiver’s decision not to pursue legal action against family members or a financial adviser over transactions that shifted millions of dollars from the retirement benefits of elderly fund members to younger family members. The facts of the case state that the receiver was appointed to the fund by orders made by the Court on 21 December 2023 following a family dispute. The initial members of the fund were Malcolm John McLennan (John) and Susan Karen Jeannine McLennan (Karen). John and Karen were husband and wife. Karen passed away on or about 2 March 2022. John and Karen remained the sole members of the fund until 2018. From in or about 2018, their son, Ruskin Dudley McLennan (Ruskin), and his partner, Jodie Elizabeth Ryan (Jodie) also became members of the fund. John and Karen have another child, Susannah McLean (Susannah), who has never been a member of the Fund. The facts continued that in or about 2018, John and Karen sought financial planning and related advice from a financial adviser. At that time, they had both passed retirement age and were retired. Under the terms of the fund, they were entitled to receive lump sum payments in the nature of a pension payment, if they so desired. At the relevant time, the assets of the fund were at least $7.5 million.
items.ai_summary: Court case highlights court-appointed receiver's decision not to pursue legal action against family members or adviser in intergenerational wealth transfer dispute

items.title: FAAA urges Treasury to refine trust tax before it becomes law
items.teaser: In its submission to Treasury regarding draft legislation for the minimum tax on discretionary trusts, the FAAA has argued that greater refinement is needed as trustees are being asked to make major and largely irreversible decisions before the full regime is settled.
items.brief_text: In its submission to Treasury regarding draft legislation for the minimum tax on discretionary trusts, the FAAA has argued that greater refinement is needed as trustees are being asked to make major and largely irreversible decisions before the full regime is settled. The package had improved on the original proposal, FAAA chief executive Sarah Abood said, but significant concerns remained. Many advice practices are themselves owned through discretionary trust structures, and advisers are also supporting clients caught by the changes. “Trustees are still required to consider making major and largely irreversible structural decisions before the full regime is settled, with further legislation, administrative requirements and guidance yet to be released,” Abood said. Trustees face three pathways under the changes; they can stay within the minimum tax regime; elect into the Excluded Election Trust (EET) model; or restructure under a transitional roll-over. Further legislation is still expected on residency, capital gains tax, international taxation and administration, leaving trustees to choose without knowing how the wider framework will work. That uncertainty adds to compliance costs already weighing on advice businesses. “The proposed reforms will impose substantial implementation and ongoing compliance costs on discretionary trust users and their advisers,” Abood said.
items.ai_summary: FAAA urges Treasury to refine trust tax legislation due to uncertainty and compliance costs for trustees and advisers

items.title: Antares Equities veteran resigns ahead of Janus Henderson takeover
items.teaser: Antares Equities' portfolio manager and head of fundamentals will conclude a long-serving tenure at the firm and will not transition to its soon-to-be parent company Janus Henderson.
items.brief_text: Antares Equities' portfolio manager and head of fundamentals will conclude a long-serving tenure at the firm and will not transition to its soon-to-be parent company Janus Henderson. John Guadagnuolo has been with Antares Equities for 18 years. He joined Antares in 2007 when it was Portfolio Partners as an investment manager, working with Andrew Hamilton, who was the head of research at the time. Hamilton was appointed to his current role of head of implementation in 2021. Guadagnuolo previously worked at Equity Trustees where he developed and ran the Australian equity research and portfolio construction processes. He was the portfolio manager of the EQT Flagship Fund, operational head of the asset management team and a member of the investment management committee where he was responsible for asset allocation research. Guadagnuolo was the portfolio manager of the Ex-20 Australian Equities Fund , which has now terminated, and the Ex-20 Model Portfolio. For the Elite Opportunities Fund, he serves as deputy portfolio manager. While core investment team members are moving to Janus Henderson, three members including Guadagnuolo, will not transition, Antares said in an investor note. "This corporate transition does not affect either the Antares Fixed Income or Fairview Equity Partners businesses," Antares wrote.
items.ai_summary: Antares Equities veteran portfolio manager resigns and will not transition to parent company Janus Henderson

items.title: Netwealth to Acquire Paradino
items.teaser: Technology and super platform, Netwealth has announced it will acquire AI automation and productivity platform, Paradino.
items.brief_text: Technology and super platform, Netwealth has announced it will acquire AI automation and productivity platform, Paradino. A message released by Netwealth CEO and Joint MD, Matt Heine, says the joint mission of the two firms is to provide advisers with the tools to automate and streamline their advice process enabling them to scale, drive efficiency
items.ai_summary: Netwealth to acquire Paradino to enhance tools for advisers to automate and streamline advice processes

items.title: IGR predicts drawdowns will be major source of retirement income
items.teaser: The report states that drawing down accumulated superannuation will become an increasingly significant part of retirement income for many retirees and is estimated to increase from 2.5 per cent of GDP in 2025–26 to 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2065–66.
items.brief_text: The report states that drawing down accumulated superannuation will become an increasingly significant part of retirement income for many retirees and is estimated to increase from 2.5 per cent of GDP in 2025–26 to 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2065–66. The proportion of people with accounts in the retirement phase, from which they are drawing a superannuation pension, will increase 13.9 percentage points (from 11.6 per cent in 2025–26 to 25.5 per cent in 2065–66). By comparison, the proportion of the population over 65 will increase by only seven percentage points (from 17.8 per cent to 24.8 per cent). “The purpose of the superannuation system is to ensure a dignified retirement. A continued policy focus that encourages accumulated superannuation savings to be drawn on effectively during retirement will help to fulfill the goal of supplementing the Age Pension as a source of retirement income and drive higher living standards in retirement,” the report stated. “The superannuation system will support a higher standard of living in retirement and reduce reliance on the Age Pension. Growing balances will result in superannuation becoming the primary source of retirement income for many retirees.” The report also noted that many recent retirees retain substantial superannuation balances at the end of their lives for multiple reasons, including complexities of navigating the superannuation system, the fear of exhausting savings and the “nest egg” framing of superannuation.
items.ai_summary: IGR report predicts drawdowns from superannuation will become a major source of retirement income, increasing significantly by 2065–66

items.title: ‘Culture eats strategy for breakfast’: Esencia on maintaining culture in interstate M&A
items.teaser: After expanding into Queensland for the first time this year, Sydney-based Esencia’s head Matthew Fenning has shared his tips for ensuring culture remains consistent interstate.
items.brief_text: After expanding into Queensland for the first time this year, Sydney-based Esencia’s head Matthew Fenning has shared his tips for ensuring culture remains consistent interstate. Esencia was founded in 2024 and recently completed its first interstate acquisition by striking a multi-merger deal with Financial 3 Wealth and Marsden Wealth Advisers in Queensland, bringing four new financial advisers and around 300 clients under its domain. A further six people have since been added to the team since the merger completed. Although it had completed multiple acquisitions already, this was the first time it had carried out one outside of its home state of New South Wales. The firm is aiming to serve 8,000 to 10,000 clients within five years and currently has 24 authorised representatives working with 2,800 clients, up from 11 advisers and 1,000 clients back in March. Esencia has previously stated there are three pillars it considers regarding any M&A activity: a focus on world-class client outcomes; being a great workplace for hard-working people; and innovation that helps advisers spend more time with their clients. Speaking to Money Management, chief executive Fenning said ensuring a consistent culture is one of the most important aspects of conducting M&A activity and can make or break a potential deal.
items.ai_summary: Esencia shares tips on maintaining culture during interstate M&A after its first acquisition outside New South Wales

items.title: CPA urges super funds to solve retirement phase or risk locking trillions out of the economy
items.teaser: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said the new Retirement Standard from Association of Super Funds Australia comes amid concerns that many retirees are reluctant to draw on their super savings, despite Australia managing one of the world’s largest retirement asset pools.
items.brief_text: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said the new Retirement Standard from Association of Super Funds Australia comes amid concerns that many retirees are reluctant to draw on their super savings, despite Australia managing one of the world’s largest retirement asset pools. “That’s exactly what the retirement standard measures. It focuses on the income retirees need to fund a comfortable or modest lifestyle, not simply the amount of super they have accumulated,” he said. Webb said Australia’s superannuation system had delivered impressive results and has helped build a retirement savings pool of around $4.5 trillion, but the retirement phase remained a major weakness. “For all the success of Australia’s superannuation system in building one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings, the industry continues to struggle with the most important transition of all: paying members an income when they retire,” he said. “The uncomfortable reality is that super funds have become very good at collecting contributions and growing balances, but far less effective at helping retirees convert those balances into sustainable income streams that they feel comfortable spending.” Research from ASIC in 2025 highlighted a lack of consistency on how retirees should be supported in retirement, with no agreed best-practice approach to retirement income products, retirement income strategies or large-scale advice delivery.
items.ai_summary: CPA urges super funds to address retirement phase challenges to ensure retirees can access their super savings effectively

items.title: Pacific AM to land SMA solutions Down Under, appoints investment chief
items.teaser: Pacific Portfolio Solutions, the related body corporate of Pacific Asset Management, will bring the latter's SMA solutions to Australia from the UK, welcoming an industry stalwart to chart the course.
items.brief_text: Pacific Portfolio Solutions (PPS), the related body corporate of Pacific Asset Management (PAM), will bring the latter's separately managed account (SMA) solutions to Australia from the UK, welcoming an industry stalwart to chart the course. Both PPS and PAM are wholly owned subsidiaries of the ASX-listed Pinnacle Investment Management. The initial PPS offering will include the Pinnacle SMA range, comprising Moderate, Balanced, Income, Growth, High Growth, and Listed Growth portfolios, built exclusively from Pinnacle affiliates' actively managed strategies, the firm said. PAM chief executive Matt Lamb said he is looking forward to bringing those capabilities to Australia. "We're bringing something distinctive to Australian managed accounts with PAM's proven multi-asset process and implementation technology," Lamb said. "Being part of the broader Pinnacle group uniquely positions the team to draw on the breadth of expertise across the group's high-quality affiliated fund managers and the strength of its institutional infrastructure." To support the launch, PPS has appointed former Perpetual chief investment officer Kyle Lidbury to lead it Australia-based investment team. Financial Standard reported on the appointment in March , but Pinnacle did not disclose his position at the time. In the newly created role of chief investment officer, Lidbury will oversee PPS' managed account portfolio construction, asset allocation, and adviser investment communications.
items.ai_summary: Pacific AM will introduce SMA solutions to Australia and appoints Kyle Lidbury as chief investment officer

items.title: Rest director for product departs
items.teaser: The general manager, product at Rest has left the super fund after nearly four years.
items.brief_text: The general manager, product at Rest has left the super fund after nearly four years. Scott Tully has departed the $113 billion fund after a close to four-year stint. He joined Rest as head of investment option development in March 2023 on a contract basis before being appointed to general manager, product a year later . Tully was most notable for his time at Colonial First State, spanning over two decades at the company across various leadership positions, including general manager, investments, head of investments, and head of FirstChoice investments before joining Rest. He also served as portfolio manager at Commonwealth Investment Management, the investment advice arm of Commonwealth Bank in 2002 earlier in his career. He shared his departure on LinkedIn, stating he has finished a "very rewarding" tenure at the fund. "It was an enjoyable time defined by great people, purposeful work and a strong focus on Rest's members. My thanks to Andrew Lill, and Deborah Potts for the opportunities they put to me, and to the fantastic teams I had the privilege to work with," Tully said. "A particular thanks to the product team for teaching me all things product (including a deep dive into Insurance). Their enthusiasm and focus made it a pleasure, and I'm proud that together we made Rest's investment menu and default insurance Super Simple.
items.ai_summary: Rest's general manager, product, Scott Tully, has departed after nearly four years at the super fund

items.title: Praemium brings forward chair succession
items.teaser: Praemium will bring forward its leadership transition at board level, with its current chair stepping down as the platform and portfolio administration business continues to expand its focus on high-net-worth investors and technology.
items.brief_text: Praemium will bring forward its leadership transition at board level, with its current chair stepping down as the platform and portfolio administration business continues to expand its focus on high-net-worth investors and technology. Matthew Quinn will replace Barry Lewin as chair, with Lewin bringing forward his departure and stepping down from the role effective 22 September 2026. Praemium said Lewin had overseen significant growth during his tenure, with the board thanking him for his contribution, leadership and commitment to the company and its people. Quinn was first appointed as non-executive director earlier this year. Initially, Quinn was set to succeed Lewin as chair at the conclusion of AGM scheduled for November. The change comes as Praemium continues to focus on building growth across its platform and non-custodial portfolio administration businesses while responding to changing expectations among high-net-worth investors. Research from Praemium and Core Data published in August found 80% of high-net-worth investors who work with an adviser had already used artificial intelligence (AI) for financial tasks, including financial education, comparing investment strategies and sense-checking advice. However, only 29% said they would manage their portfolio themselves if given access to the same tools as their adviser, while roughly seven in 10 would still prefer to retain their adviser's guidance.
items.ai_summary: Praemium accelerates chair succession as it expands focus on high-net-worth investors and technology

items.title: Advisers missing the third retirement risk, warns Aged Care Steps
items.teaser: Aged Care Steps is urging advisers to plan for frailty risk alongside longevity and sequencing risk, after its latest whitepaper found older Australians are spending more of their retirement with severe disability.
items.brief_text: Aged Care Steps is urging advisers to plan for frailty risk alongside longevity and sequencing risk, after its latest whitepaper found older Australians are spending more of their retirement with severe disability. It’s Planning for the Third Phase of Retirement report found the expected period of severe disability for a man aged 65 rose from 3.5 years in 2018 to 4.6 years in 2022, or from 17.5 per cent to 22 per cent of retirement. Women saw the period rise from 5.5 to 6.4 years, or from 25 per cent to 28 per cent of retirement. “During the frailty period, the rising incidence of dementia, increasing care costs and greater burden on family are making aged care decisions more complex and consequential, creating both a client need and an advice opportunity,” Aged Care Steps director Assyat David said. Aged Care Steps estimates the frailty years make up 17 to 24 per cent of retirement on average and said income needs are more likely to follow a U-shape than the straight-line retirement plans have typically used. The average refundable accommodation deposit has risen 15 per cent in 18 months to $604,919, according to the paper, while the maximum permissible interest rate for daily accommodation payment has gone from 7.78 per cent to 8.43 per cent in a year. In one case study, a single homeowner with approximately $1.2 million in assets moves into a $605,000 room and pays by daily accommodation payment rather than a lump sum.
items.ai_summary: Advisers are urged to plan for frailty risk in retirement alongside longevity and sequencing risk due to increased severe disability periods.

items.title: Retirement confidence lags as investors turn to AI
items.teaser: Retirement has emerged as a central for investors globally, but a lack of confidence and financial literacy is keeping many savers on the sidelines, according to Amundi's latest global investor study.
items.brief_text: Retirement has emerged as a central concern for investors globally, but a lack of confidence and financial literacy is keeping many savers on the sidelines, according to Amundi's latest global investor study. The third edition of Amundi's Decoding Investors study surveyed 17,000 respondents across 26 countries and found personal savings and investments are expected to provide 42% of investor's retirement income, ahead of state provisions and workplace pensions. However, only 23% of investors said they were very confident about achieving long-term financial security, down from 26% a year earlier. Professional advice is a significant factor in retirement confidence, with half of advised investors saying they were very confident about funding retirement, compared with 14% of those who have never accessed advice. Amundi found 43% of savers expected to start investing within the next 12 months, rising to 62% among those aged 21 to 30. However, 39% said fear of losing money remained a barrier, contributing to continued high cash holdings. The study also highlighted a gap between perceived and actual investment knowledge, with 70% of investors who described themselves as experts failing to correctly answer three basic financial literacy questions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of investors decision making, with 70% saying they had used AI to help make investment decisions. Of those, 59% had acted on AI recommendations.
items.ai_summary: A study shows low retirement confidence and financial literacy are keeping many investors from engaging, with AI becoming a common tool in investment decisions.

items.title: UBS appoints ‘head of purpose’ in not-for-profit shake-up
items.teaser: UBS is renaming its not-for-profit segment to a ‘for purpose’ division as Anthony Hamawi is appointed from JBWere to head up the department. Hamawi will be joining UBS in mid-October as head of for purpose organisations, reporting to Wayne Gordon (head of advisory & sales, Australia).
items.brief_text: UBS is renaming its not-for-profit segment to a ‘for purpose’ division as Anthony Hamawi is appointed from JBWere to head up the department. Hamawi will be joining UBS in mid-October as head of for purpose organisations, reporting to Wayne Gordon (head of advisory & sales, Australia). Melbourne-based Hamawi’s role as head of for purpose organisations will include making sure UBS actions remain relevant to the bank’s purpose. “[Hamawi] will help us continue to evolve our client proposition to ensure we are delivering advice and solutions that are aligned with the unique needs, objectives, and impact ambitions of these organisations,” said Andrew Bird, head of global wealth management Australia. He joins UBS from JBWere, where he was a director for over a year and a half, and member of the Philanthropic Services team. There, he collaborated with not-for-profits, foundations, charities, and philanthropic families. Before that, he worked for almost 10 years at Perpetual in Melbourne. He was involved with social impact, not-for-profit and aged care organisations. This is the third senior appointment UBS has made from JBWere following the hire of Bird and Damian Robinson in July as market team head . UBS affirmed that not-for-profit remains an important segment but said the name change reflects the breadth of organisations with social impact that it supports.
items.ai_summary: UBS is rebranding its not-for-profit segment to 'for purpose' and appointing Anthony Hamawi to lead the division, reflecting a broader focus on social impact organizations.

items.title: Vietnam joins FTSE Russell emerging market index
items.teaser: Vietnam has officially joined the FTSE Russell Global Equity Index Series, marking a new phase for its capital market as it moves from frontier to Secondary Emerging Market status.
items.brief_text: Vietnam has officially joined the FTSE Russell Global Equity Index Series, marking a new phase for its capital market as it moves from frontier to Secondary Emerging Market status. The reclassification took effect on 21 September 2026, following years of reforms to Vietnam's market infrastructure, regulatory framework and access for international investors. The milestone was marked at a conference in Hanoi attended by 200 delegates, including representatives from global investment firms, custodians, securities companies and other market participants. Vietnam Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan said the reclassification would broaden access to international capital while raising expectations around market quality and regulatory capacity. "Vietnam is ready to listen to international organisations and pursue further bold reforms to build a transparent, safe, and efficient capital market that remains sustainably attractive," Tuan said. The government intends to continue capital market development through 2030, with a longer-term vision to 2045, including measures to improve liquidity, modernise infrastructure, strengthen risk management and diversify investment products. UK ambassador to Vietnam Iain Grant Frew said the reclassification reflected the country's economic transformation and efforts to build a deeper and more internationally connected capital market.
items.ai_summary: Vietnam has been reclassified from frontier to secondary emerging market status in the FTSE Russell index, signaling improved market infrastructure and regulatory reforms.

items.title: Equity Trustees responds to takeover bids
items.teaser: Equity Trustees has responded to two separate takeover bids received by the firm last month. On 21 August, the firm received a proposal from Melbourne private equity firm BGH Capital for $24.75 cash per share.
items.brief_text: Equity Trustees has responded to two separate takeover bids received by the firm last month. On 21 August, the firm received a proposal from Melbourne private equity firm BGH Capital for $24.75 cash per share. Founded in 2017, BGH Capital is an independent private equity firm which invests in businesses in Australia and New Zealand with strong fundamentals and growing end markets. This followed an earlier proposal made to EQT on 17 August from global asset manager TPG Global for $24.55 cash per share, a far larger player than BGH with US$327 billion ($458 billion) in assets under management. Both firms have stated the indicative offer price under their respective Proposals will not be reduced by the FY26 final dividend of 20 cents per share announced by Equity Trustees and their respective proposals are not conditional on Equity Trustees implementing an exit of the Superannuation Trustee Services business or the conclusion of the ASIC litigation. In an ASX statement on 21 September, EQT said: “The EQT board, with input from management and legal and financial advisers, has carefully considered the proposals. The board has also considered feedback on the proposals from shareholders. The EQT board is prepared to engage with TPG and BGH.” However, it is seeking a revised offer as it does not believe the current one reflects the firm’s value and has granted both parties provision of non-public information to aide this.
items.ai_summary: Equity Trustees is reviewing two takeover bids, seeking a revised offer that better reflects the firm's value and is not conditional on certain business exits or litigation outcomes.

items.title: How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang could reshape geopolitics for investors
items.teaser: Stanford University professor Stephen Kotkin says computing power will become the key geopolitical contest between the US and China, predicting Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang will become an increasingly central figure in international relations.
items.brief_text: Computing power, not broad economic sanctions, is the one lever historian Stephen Kotkin argues the US can pull that might actually work against China. In a keynote address to the Top1000funds.com Fiduciary Investors Symposium at Stanford University, Kotkin suggested Nvidia’s Jensen Huang could be the one figure whose next move reshapes that balance. Kotkin, who is the Kleinheinz Senior Fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, said the US position in computing power is the exception to his general scepticism about sanctions. “We’ve got about 75 per cent going to 80 per cent of computing power in the United States,” he said. “I would be seduced into thinking that’s a big trend line where money is going to be made, not just tomorrow, but maybe after tomorrow.” That dominance matters, he added, “for as long as computing power is the limiting factor in AI”, though he was careful to note he does not know how long that will remain true. But “there are many places” where broad economic sanctions could backfire, or only have “a temporary impact, if any, with perverse and unintended consequences,” he said. “It reduces trust in the dollar.” Prior to his address to the symposium, Kotkin met with Conexus Financial founder Colin Tate AM and chair Geoff Lloyd in his Hoover Tower office on campus at Stanford and expanded on the implications of the geopolitical landscape for investors. Shifting ground In his symposium address, Kotkin cautioned that the compute advantage is not static.
items.ai_summary: Computing power dominance in the US could reshape geopolitical dynamics for investors, according to historian Stephen Kotkin.

items.title: The New Class of Adviser: Vertical integration and the case for advice practices
items.teaser: On 19 August, Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino announced, among other reforms, that the government would push ahead the ‘New Class of Adviser’ (NCA), but they would be limited to superannuation funds and insurance providers.
items.brief_text: On 19 August, Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino announced, among other reforms, that the government would push ahead the ‘New Class of Adviser’ (NCA), but they would be limited to superannuation funds and insurance providers. The FAAA has long argued that, should NCAs be introduced, that advice practices should be allowed to employ them in order to support the industry in delivering scoped or simple advice. Phil Anderson, FAAA general manager of policy, advocacy and standards, said the association was “disappointed with the outcome”, but said that there was still hope that advice practices may be rolled into the program in three years, when the minister has committed to a review of the stipulation. There isn’t a solid explanation at this point as to why they were left out, however FAAA chief executive Sarah Abood suggested it may be down to an abundance of caution while the government understands how NCAs will operate in practice. “I think the minister is aware or has a view that this is a very new thing, and his instinct was to kind of start small and then maybe grow it over time. But he wasn’t explicit in the speech about the thinking behind it, so I’m meta-analysing what he said,” Abood told an FAAA roundtable attended by ifa.
items.ai_summary: The government has limited the 'New Class of Adviser' to superannuation funds and insurance providers, with potential for advice practices to be included in the future.

items.title: FAAA flags gaps in discretionary trusts tax reforms, deficient framework
items.teaser: Under the proposed minimum tax on discretionary trust reforms, the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) highlighted concerns over trustees potentially being forced to make "major and largely irreversible decisions" before the rules and guidance have been finalised.
items.brief_text: Under the proposed minimum tax on discretionary trust reforms, the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) highlighted concerns over trustees potentially being forced to make "major and largely irreversible decisions" before the rules and guidance have been finalised. Treasury released the draft legislation on the 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts in early September, consulting on how the minimum tax will work, what types of trusts and income should be excluded and how a fixed trust should be defined. One of the proposed changes is introducing a new option for discretionary trusts to be exempt from the minimum tax if they elect to make fixed distributions to pre-nominated beneficiaries, as an alternative to roll-over relief. The election would not require a restructure and is not expected to result in state and territory stamp duties. Trustees will also be able to nominate individuals and entities that are capable of benefiting under the trust from 1 July 2028, including eligible companies and trusts, with no limit on the number of beneficiaries that can be nominated. The association believes some of the new pathways proposed are too rigid and could unfairly penalise people who make genuine mistakes or experience normal life events such as family changes, succession planning or circumstances beyond their control.
items.ai_summary: FAAA warns of potential unfair penalties for trustees under proposed discretionary trusts tax reforms due to rigid rules and lack of clarity.

items.title: What the 2026 Intergenerational Report means for advisers
items.teaser: Focus Partners Australia says this week’s Intergenerational Report highlights a world where Aussies will be living longer and retirement last longer.
items.brief_text: Focus Partners Australia says this week’s Intergenerational Report highlights a world where Aussies will be living longer and retirement last longer. According to the government’s 2026 Intergenerational Report, life expectancy in Australia is projected to reach almost 90 years for women and just over 86.1 years for men by 2066. Released on 21 September, the report projects the outlook for the Australian economy and the Government’s budget to 2065–66. These projections help inform and improve public policy settings to better position Australia for the next 40 years. Meanwhile, the number of Australians aged 85 and over is expected to triple, with consequences for retirement planning amid increased healthcare and aged care considerations. Focus also pointed to more complex wealth transfer decisions if retirement lasts longer. This means that proactive financial planning is even more important, according to Focus Partners Australia. For now, the advice firm says the superannuation system has been effective in building wealth during the accumulation phase of older Aussies. In fact, the report predicts that the proportion of older Australians receiving an Age Pension or income support payment will fall from 66 per cent currently to 52 per cent in 40 years.
items.ai_summary: The 2026 Intergenerational Report predicts Australians will live longer, leading to extended retirements and increased complexity in wealth transfer and retirement planning.

items.title: Beyond traditional bucketing: Why advisers are rethinking SMSF retirement strategies
items.teaser: Retirement bucketing strategies have long been a cornerstone of SMSF retirement planning, helping retirees manage sequencing risk by separating short-term spending needs from longer-term growth assets.
items.brief_text: Retirement bucketing strategies have long been a cornerstone of SMSF retirement planning, helping retirees manage sequencing risk by separating short-term spending needs from longer-term growth assets. But new actuarial research suggests advisers may be overlooking an important piece of the retirement income puzzle: guaranteed lifetime income. At a recent webinar hosted by Money Management with Allianz Retire+ , advisers heard how combining traditional bucketing strategies with lifetime income solutions could materially improve retirement outcomes for SMSF members. Independent modelling conducted by Accurium tested more than 3,000 retirement strategy scenarios and found consistent improvements in both retirement income confidence and projected estate values when lifetime income was incorporated into a retirement framework. According to Melanie Dunn, head of actuarial services at Accurium, the findings challenge some of the conventional assumptions underpinning retirement portfolio construction. “The objective of the research was to assess whether retirement bucketing strategies incorporating a lifetime income solution could improve retirement outcomes for SMSF members when compared with more traditional retirement approaches,” she said. The research comes at a time when advisers are being asked to solve increasingly complex retirement challenges.
items.ai_summary: Advisers are rethinking SMSF retirement strategies by incorporating guaranteed lifetime income solutions to improve retirement outcomes.

items.title: CPA worried more people will seek financial advice
items.teaser: Certified Practicing Accountants (CPA) Australia have warned that government changes to discretionary trusts could cost Australians up to $2.8 billion in advice fees due to uncertainty.
items.brief_text: Certified Practicing Accountants (CPA) Australia have warned that government changes to discretionary trusts could cost Australians up to $2.8 billion in advice fees due to uncertainty. The CPA said that while it supports the policy objective of the 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, its submission to treasury outlines some of the key elements it says will create unintended c onsequences for family businesses, trustees and beneficiaries. The peak body stated that, under the exposure draft, discretionary trusts existing on 1 July 2028 can elect into a regime that would avoid the minimum tax and the need to restructure as a company. The election can only be made once during the 2028–29 income year and cannot be reversed. “Treasury has costed this on around 350,000 small businesses. But 850,000 discretionary trusts lodge a return each year, and every one of those trustees has to decide whether to elect – because if you don’t decide, you’ve decided,” CPA tax lead Jenny Wong said. “On our modelling, the cost of professional advice alone is between $2 to $2.8 billion. That’s incurred before anyone restructures, and whether or not a single trust elects. It’s the cost of working out the answer, not the cost of complying with it. “This isn’t the cost of paying the tax. It’s the cost of working out what to do about it”.
items.ai_summary: CPA warns government changes to discretionary trusts could lead to $2.8 billion in advice fees due to uncertainty

items.title: The ‘kids’ inheriting older clients’ wealth might soon be retirees themselves
items.teaser: The conventional wisdom that the kids of advisers’ oldest clients stand to inherit their wealth might be overlooking the fact that by the time it happens these “kids” are likely to be near or in retirement themselves.
items.brief_text: For as long as most advisers can remember, one assumption has underpinned almost every business growth plan: an older client’s wealth will eventually pass to their children, and those children will need an adviser of their own. But that assumption may have a flaw, or at least a wrinkle, as revealed by Treasury’s 2026 Intergenerational Report , released on Monday. The “kids” who stand to inherit the older clients’ wealth are getting older too. Treasury’s report suggests that as clients get older, by the time their estate is actually settled their children are themselves likely to already in their late 50s or into their 60s, well established in their own careers and in fact closer to their own retirement than to buying a first home. They may be in less need of inherited wealth than their own children. So, if an advice business really wants to “freshen up” its client base by attracting younger clients just starting out on their financial journey, then maybe the onboarding efforts need to be directed at the next generation but one: the grandchildren. The Treasury report paints a clear picture of a population getting older and wealthier, and the challenges this poses both at a national level and to the financial advisers whose role is so critical to helping Australians manage both aging and getting richer. It projects Australian women will live to 89.5 years and men to 86.1 by 2065-66, with the 85-and-over cohort set to triple in size over the same period.
items.ai_summary: Treasury's report indicates inheriting clients' wealth may soon go to retirees rather than younger generations

items.title: ART-owned G'day Group invests $200m in regional holiday parks
items.teaser: Australian Retirement Trust (ART) owned G'day Group plans to invest more than $200 million in regional holiday parks in the lead up to the 2032 Olympic Games.
items.brief_text: Australian Retirement Trust (ART) owned G'day Group plans to invest more than $200 million in regional holiday parks in the lead up to the 2032 Olympic Games. G'day Group will expand 12 of its regional Queensland discovery parks and resorts, including a $20 million upgrade of discovery parks in Townsville. This comes as ART's board and senior leaders meet in Townsville this week. G'day Group chief executive Grant Wilckens said there is a growing demand for high-quality holiday parks and resorts before the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games. "We have invested more than $110 million across regional Queensland over the last three years including the acquisition of eco-tourism destination, Habitat Noosa, earlier this year," Wilckens said. The $20 million upgrade of discovery parks in Townsville will include 30 new cabins and 30 sites, plus new visitor facilities, building on a $5 million investment G'day Group recently completed which delivered 18 new cabins. "Together, these upgrades will expand the park's accommodation offering and increase capacity to support growing visitation to the region for major events and local attractions," he added.
items.ai_summary: ART-owned G'day Group plans $200 million investment in regional holiday parks ahead of 2032 Olympics

items.title: Questions raised about how ATO will deal with investment strategy documentation
items.teaser: In a Q&A session at the ASF Audit Technical Seminar last week, Burgess said if SMSF trustees are now going to have to provide the ATO with investment strategies, he questioned what it will be looking for in its reviews of them.
items.brief_text: In a Q&A session at the ASF Audit Technical Seminar last week, Burgess said if SMSF trustees are now going to have to provide the ATO with investment strategies, he questioned what it will be looking for in its reviews of them. “I would expect that one of the things it will be looking at is diversification. There have been issues in the past where an SMSF has a substantial amount of their balance in a property, for example, but when you consider the other circumstances, that is not unreasonable,” Burgess said. “We also know that for self-managed super funds, the strategy they put in place recognises that, and they’re using future contributions to diversify. That’s all part of a legitimate strategy. “That’s why we’re concerned if the ATO is going to start to receive these investment strategies, what actually they are going to do with these? Because they are not a prudential supervisor which is a regulator that actually has control over where you invest, essentially, or making sure that the fund is making appropriate decisions around investments and diversification. That’s not the ATO.” Jo Hurley, Head of Technical for ASF Audits, said auditors already look at investment strategies each year. “We are certainly looking at those investment strategies every year.
items.ai_summary: Questions raised about ATO's role in reviewing SMSF investment strategies

items.title: Fewer, clearer decisions: Hamilton Wealth takes the OCIO route
items.teaser: An idea that started with a conversation in New York has led to Hamilton Wealth Partners opt for an outsourced chief investment officer (OCIO) arrangement.
items.brief_text: A year ago in New York, Hamilton Wealth Partners founder and chief executive officer Will Hamilton sat down with an US outsourced chief investment officer (OCIO) firm to learn more about how it worked, and part of that conversation stuck with him. “There was one comment they made, that the problem with a lot of firms is their APLs become a byproduct of what they’ve been sold,” Hamilton tells Professional Planner . “Those were the words they used, and I thought that’s a really interesting comment. So, I just looked into the space a lot more.” Hamilton says he “hadn’t really heard of [the OCIO concept], to be honest” before the New York conversation. “We had noted the… the amount of product that was becoming available and being shown to us. We also looked at the geopolitical effect on markets that had occurred really since 2022, since the current Ukraine conflict occurred; our business got bigger; and so you looked at everything together, and I felt [I] needed to do something,” he says. With four advisers plus Hamilton himself looking after 142 clients and about $1.3 billion of funds under advice, HWP had considered building out an internal capability, but ultimately went down the OCIO route and spoke to six potential partners about how it could work.
items.ai_summary: Hamilton Wealth is exploring OCIO solutions to address complexity and improve decision-making.

items.title: ‘A slice of the pie’: Macquarie class action under scrutiny
items.teaser: On 17 September, Macquarie Investment Management was handed a class action on behalf of Rachelle Dessent and around 2,800 account holders who lost their superannuation in the Shield Master Fund collapse.
items.brief_text: On 17 September , Macquarie Investment Management was handed a class action on behalf of Rachelle Dessent and around 2,800 account holders who lost their superannuation in the Shield Master Fund collapse. Gordon Legal, the firm representing the action, has alleged that impacted investors haven’t been fully compensated for losses suffered after the collapse. This is despite the $321 million Macquarie paid out last year compensating members for total invested after admitting to failures related to Shield. What they have now filed for is “the growth their superannuation may have achieved if those funds remained invested elsewhere during that time, or for the distress they have suffered”. “For most Australians, superannuation is their most important asset. When your retirement savings are tied up in a failed investment, you miss out on funds that could be life changing. That’s what happened in this case. It’s time for Macquarie to pay the full amount back,” James Naughton, Gordon Legal partner and one of the leading lawyers on the case, said. The decision has since raised some eyebrows among the industry and investors alike about whether a class action is appropriate, and even more so since Netwealth was also handed draft documents for a potential class action on 21 September.
items.ai_summary: Macquarie faces scrutiny over potential undercompensation in a class action related to the Shield Master Fund collapse.

items.title: Clients’ prolonged ‘frailty years’ is a risk advisers must consider
items.teaser: Data shows that older Australians are spending a larger share of retirement with severe disability.
items.brief_text: Longevity risk, the danger of living too long and running out of money, has been the main focus of retirement planning for decades but there’s another major risk that requires greater attention. Frailty risk, which refers to the financial, personal and family consequences that arise when declining health and increasing care needs are not adequately planned for, is on the rise, with new data revealing that Australian retirees are spending more time living with a severe disability. Between 2018 and 2022, the average amount of time men over the age of 65 were expected to spend managing a severe disability jumped from 3.5 years to 4.6 years, representing a change from 17.5 per cent to 22 per cent of their retirement years. Similarly, the average amount of time women over the age of 65 were expected to spend managing a severe disability jumped from 5.5 to 6.4 years, representing a change from 25 per cent to 28 per cent of their retirement years. Financial advisers are ideally positioned to help clients understand and manage frailty risk by embedding aged care planning into their advice proposition and guiding clients to make smart decisions before a crisis occurs. With around 5 million Australians over the age of 65, aged care planning that factors in the possibility of dementia and increasing care costs is an essential service.
items.ai_summary: Advisers must consider frailty risk, as Australian retirees are spending more time with severe disabilities.

items.title: Big data could help predict the next big advice ‘calamity’
items.teaser: FAAA chief executive officer Sarah Abood wants technology to be used to head off the next disaster in the financial advice space. Predictive models offer the opportunity to use data to detect and prevent the next collapse.
items.brief_text: A disaster such as the $1.2 billion loss of retirement savings in the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian master funds could be detected earlier and potentially prevented if more players in the advice chain are able to co-operate to analyse the data they collect. “Prevention is the opportunity,” says Financial Advice Association Australia chief executive officer Sarah Abood. “I think the opportunity we have now is to get ahead of it, to use big data, use predictive models to work out where’s the next scandal and how do we stop it before it expands to hit $1 billion and 12,000 consumers. How can we find them earlier? And I think that’s where the opportunity is for us.” She says that one of the most notable features was single advisers signing thousands of statements of advice and “yet we know that the average client per adviser is somewhere around 120, give or take. So that’s an alarm bell that should have gone off and could have gone off earlier”. “There are a few different places where there are gatekeepers that have access to that data, but it’s not being used in a structured way at the moment. I think there is real potential there, and that’s the focus for us [in] those big scandals, because data will show you.” Abood says that if one adviser pulls 500 people into a single product there should be a way to monitor that and raise an alert so it can be checked.
items.ai_summary: Big data and predictive models could help detect and prevent future advice scandals.

items.title: How battles over super could rewrite long-term advice strategies
items.teaser: Australia’s superannuation framework has long been a recurring topic of debate across the political spectrum, touted as being the ‘envy of the world’, but it is also a large pool of funds – around $4.8 trillion at present – and many are looking at it as a saviour while people do it tough.
items.brief_text: Australia’s superannuation framework has long been a recurring topic of debate across the political spectrum, touted as being the ‘envy of the world’, but it is also a large pool of funds – around $4.8 trillion at present – and many are looking at it as a saviour while people do it tough. The ongoing cost of living crisis, inflation, and a brutal housing market have really brought it to the fore with Treasurer Jim Chalmers claiming the next federal election will be a “referendum” on super. Discussions reached a fever pitch, however, when One Nation put forward its policy position on super earlier this month. On 7 September, the party’s leader, Senator Pauline Hanson, said they would allow some Australians to utilise part of their superannuation to help them own a home, if they were to win the next federal election. Specifically, she proposed an opt in system that would see Australians who pay rent or have a mortgage to access 3 per cent of their compulsory super contributions redirected by the fund to the member for up to three years. Hanson said the policy is designed to “give people some breathing room” as economic pressures continue to weigh on Australians, many of whom are struggling with cost of living pressures and the dream of home ownership. “People are working hard and still struggling to get ahead. Interest rates keep rising. Rents keep climbing. Groceries, power bills, petrol and insurance are taking more and more out of the family budget.
items.ai_summary: Political debates over superannuation could influence long-term advice strategies and access to funds.

items.title: NEOS partners with Paradino
items.teaser: Life insurance provider NEOS has announced a new integration with AI automation platform Paradino to help advisers compare the pricing of protection options.
items.brief_text: Life insurance provider NEOS has announced a new integration with AI automation platform Paradino to help advisers compare the pricing of protection options. The Paradino integration has been designed to provide advisers with fast, seamless access to pricing while maintaining the important role of professional advice in delivering quality client outcomes. Paradino provides AI-generated notes, customer profiling, advice presentations, as well as workflow and task management tools. By expanding access to pricing across AI-powered adviser technology platforms, NEOS said this will help advisers compare protection options quickly and easily. This includes Encompass Protection, Futura Protection and NEOS Protection. This integration follows the recent announcement of the pricing integration through Marloo to provide advisers with access to insurance quotes and product information during the advice process, allowing them to assess options and support client discussions without leaving the platform. NEOS managing director, John de Zwart, said: “This launch is another important step in delivering on our vision to make life insurance easy. Bringing Encompass Protection, Futura Protection and NEOS Protection pricing into Paradino gives advisers greater choice in how they access insurance insights within the tools they already use.
items.ai_summary: NEOS integration with Paradino provides advisers with fast access to insurance pricing within their workflows
