items.title: Intergenerational Report looks to AI to buoy productivity slump
items.teaser: Australia's economy will continue to stagnate over the next 40 years, growing at just 2% annually, according to the latest Intergenerational Report (IGR), which points to the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution to buoy sagging productivity.
items.brief_text: Australia's economy will continue to stagnate over the next 40 years, growing at just 2% annually, according to the latest Intergenerational Report (IGR), which points to the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution to buoy sagging productivity. Treasury estimates the economy will more than double its current size and income per capita is tipped to hit 55% by 2065-66 but acknowledges that Australia's productivity performance will depend on adopting innovation, supporting investment, developing skills and delivering regulatory reforms that improve the efficient operation of the economy. The nation's real gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to slump to 2% on an average annual basis, which is below the 3% experienced over the past 40 years. However, based on a long-term productivity growth assumptions, Treasury maintains a rate of just 1.2% p.a. Slowing population growth and ageing will continue to drag on economic performance. Australians will continue to have among the longest life expectancies in the world, projected to be 89.5 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2065-66. Those aged 65 and over is projected to continue growing, while the 85-plus cohort is expected to be the fastest growing. The ageing population primarily stems from falling fertility rates, while the country's older population profile will negatively impact labour force participation.
items.ai_summary: Intergenerational Report forecasts Australia's economy to grow at 2% annually over the next 40 years, with AI seen as a key driver for productivity

items.title: Magellan terminates Vinva Global Equity fund
items.teaser: Magellan Asset Management has announced it will terminate the Vinva Global Equity fund next month. In an investor note, it said the fund had been soft closed to new investors on 17 August and is expected to be formally terminated on 12 October.
items.brief_text: Magellan Asset Management has announced it will terminate the Vinva Global Equity fund next month. In an investor note, it said the fund had been soft closed to new investors on 17 August and is expected to be formally terminated on 12 October. Magellan first announced a strategic partnership with systematic fund manager Vinva in August 2024 and acquired a 29.5 per cent stake in its parent company. The fund was launched in October 2024 and is $165.3 million in size. It aims to use a systematic investment approach to harvest returns from listed global companies and deliver consistent returns through different market environments. Since inception, the fund has returned 18.3 per cent versus returns of 14.9 per cent by the MSCI ACWI ex Australia ex Tobacco ex Controversial Weapons benchmark. Chief executive, Sophia Rahmani, said: “After careful review, we have determined that the fund has not reached sufficient scale to be sustainable over the longer term and we have decided that the intended termination of the fund is in the best interests of unitholders. “We expect to provide formal notice of the termination of the fund on or around 2 October 2026 with the termination date to be on or around 12 October 2026.” Magellan suggested investors could switch their exposure to the Vinva Global Alpha Fund – Active ETF which also has an active, systematic approach. This is the latest in several fund changes made by the firm, which recently merged with Barrenjoey Capital Partners.
items.ai_summary: Magellan Asset Management will terminate the Vinva Global Equity fund due to insufficient scale

items.title: Class expands registry capabilities to streamline SMSF administration
items.teaser: The enhancements introduce an industry-first integration for unlisted investments through Automic, new registry document feeds with MUFG Pension & Market Services, and a direct cash statement feed from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) to help SMSF professionals streamline administration and reduce the need for…
items.brief_text: The enhancements introduce an industry-first integration for unlisted investments through Automic, new registry document feeds with MUFG Pension & Market Services, and a direct cash statement feed from the Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) to help SMSF professionals streamline administration and reduce the need for manual document collection across complex SMSF portfolios. The announcement comes as SMSF professionals look to leverage automation to enhance productivity, with 44 per cent of SMSF accountants identifying workflow automation as a key capability from software providers. At the same time, unlisted assets continue to grow within SMSFs, with advisers directing 21 per cent of new inflows to active unlisted managed funds and a further 10 per cent to index unlisted managed funds. Class’s direct registry connections introduced during FY25, already cover 97 per cent of ASX-listed companies and provide ownership and holding balances for more than 2,280 listed securities. The enhanced integration with Automic delivers registry-sourced balances and supporting documents for unlisted holdings directly into Class, extending trusted ownership verification beyond listed securities, enabling SMSF professionals to meet reporting obligations more efficiently, with greater confidence and less manual effort.
items.ai_summary: Class expands registry capabilities with automation tools for SMSF administration

items.title: Something’s wrong when the biggest bill lands with the smallest players
items.teaser: Advice networks are the least “valuable” links in the wealth management chain, yet when something goes wrong they’re too often left to carry the can, even when a failure is not their fault.
items.brief_text: In July I sat in a room with five other advice licensees. Between us, we authorised 936 advisers and accounted for $48.2 billion under advice. We put our actual accounts for last financial year on the wall and added them up. This was not a survey and not a model, but six sets of real numbers. The advice relationships in those six businesses generated $741 million of revenue across the financial services chain. Of that, $416 million went to platforms, investment managers and insurers. That money never appears in an advice business’s accounts. We do not invoice it and we never see it. So, a total of $325 million arrived with the licensees. Of that, $283 million went to the advisers themselves, and $30 million went to operating costs, which is licensing, compliance, technology and professional indemnity. After that, $11 million was left, across six licensees and 936 advisers, for a year’s work. The chart below plots each segment’s valuation multiple against measured risk. Platforms carry the lowest risk and trade at about 95 times earnings; listed advice businesses trade at about 11 times on the same measure; advisory networks carry the highest risk and the lowest multiple. I used to call that pricing revenue rather than risk. I no longer think that is right, or platforms would carry the heaviest rating.
items.ai_summary: Analysis reveals significant financial disparity between platforms and advisers in the advice industry

items.title: CGT overhaul could reshape super contribution strategies
items.teaser: Formica said while complying super funds will retain access to existing CGT concessions, gains realised by individuals and distributed through trusts could face a new regime featuring cost-based indexation and a 30 per cent minimum tax rate, potentially reducing the effectiveness of deductible super contributions as a…
items.brief_text: Formica said while complying super funds will retain access to existing CGT concessions, gains realised by individuals and distributed through trusts could face a new regime featuring cost-based indexation and a 30 per cent minimum tax rate, potentially reducing the effectiveness of deductible super contributions as a tax-planning tool. “The changes to the CGT rules, changes to the taxation of trusts, are going to impact contribution strategies in the future,” she said. “To start with, the changes to the CGT which in the main have already been legislated will start on 1 July, 27. CGT assets are when an individual realises a capital gain in their own name because they owned that asset directly, or maybe they were a partner in a partnership, or it could even be a trust that owns the asset and they distribute that gain through to an individual. “We also have to bear in mind there are some exemptions to the changes where we’ve got new residential dwellings and affordable housing.” Formica said the rule changes that will apply going forward depend on when a client has bought and sold an asset relative to 1 July 2027. If the asset was bought and sold prior to that date, they will be subject to the current CGT rules. If it was bought and sold on or after 1 July 2027, they will be subject to the new rules. “For assets which were bought before 1 July 2027 but sold on or after 1 July 2027, it is a mix of the old and new rules,” Formica said.
items.ai_summary: CGT overhaul may impact super contribution strategies with new tax rules starting 1 July 2027

items.title: Definition of trust needs to be ‘crystal clear’ warns SMSFA
items.teaser: In its submission to Treasury on the exposure draft, the SMSFA said a significant concern for SMSFs and broader superannuation sector is the potential emergence of two separate and inconsistent tests for determining when trust income should receive concessional superannuation taxation treatment.
items.brief_text: In its submission to Treasury on the exposure draft, the SMSFA said a significant concern for SMSFs and broader superannuation sector is the potential emergence of two separate and inconsistent tests for determining when trust income should receive concessional superannuation taxation treatment. “A trust may be classified as a minimum tax trust because it does not satisfy the existing fixed trust concepts derived from Schedule 2F. However, superannuation fund taxation outcomes under section 295-550 are based on a separate question: whether the fund holds a ‘fixed entitlement’ to trust income for the purposes of the non-arm’s length income (NALI) provisions,” it said. “As recognised by existing ATO guidance, these are not necessarily the same tests. The Commissioner of Taxation’s Taxation Ruling TR 2006/711 has set out the guiding principles for the past 20 years on what constitutes a ‘fixed entitlement’ and as such has been heavily relied upon by the SMSF sector. It has continued in force despite the repeal of the original special income provisions and replaced by the non-arm’s length income regime.” It added that any departure from this longstanding interpretation could result in widespread and unintended changes to the taxation outcomes of established superannuation and SMSF investment structures.
items.ai_summary: SMSFA warns of potential inconsistencies in trust definitions affecting superannuation taxation

items.title: Early bird pricing closing soon for FAAA Congress 2026
items.teaser: Early bird pricing for this year’s Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) Congress will close on 30 September.
items.brief_text: Early bird pricing for this year’s Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) Congress will close on 30 September. The Congress, being held in Melbourne from 24 to 26 November, will have the theme ‘Explore’, reflecting the FAAA’s commitment to equipping financial advisers with practical strategies, technical expertise, and fresh thinking to navigate an evolving profession. Currently, FAAA member tickets are $1,305 and non-member tickets are $2,695. Once early bird registration closes full price members are $1,650 and non-member tickets are $2,995. The Congress features an impressive keynote line-up, with internationally recognised investor and engineer Dr Jordan Nguyen opening the event to explore how curiosity, innovation, and emerging technologies are reshaping what’s possible. The Congress will close with Melbourne Cup-winning jockey Michelle Payne in conversation with Emmy Award-winning journalist Sara James, sharing lessons in resilience, leadership, and achieving success against the odds. FAAA chair David Sharpe says Congress is the highlight of the FAAA’s calendar and the place where Australia’s advice profession comes together. “The early pricing represents a significant saving, and I strongly encourage those planning to attend to purchase their tickets before 30 September,” Sharpe says. “This year’s program has been carefully curated to cover the issues shaping the future of financial advice.
items.ai_summary: Early bird pricing for FAAA Congress 2026 closes on 30 September with discounted member rates
